params.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a medico-legal autopsy from a clinical (hospital) autopsy?

answers.text: A clinical autopsy requires police authorisation, while a medico-legal autopsy requires consent of relatives

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. It is the other way round — medico-legal autopsies are conducted under statutory authority without consent; clinical autopsies require consent of relatives.

answers.text: A medico-legal autopsy is conducted under statutory authority without consent, while a clinical autopsy requires consent and serves diagnostic purposes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The medico-legal autopsy is ordered under statutory authority (e.g., CrPC Section 174) and does not require consent — its purpose is forensic and legal. The clinical autopsy is hospital-based, consent-dependent, and serves diagnostic or audit purposes.

answers.text: Both types of autopsy require consent of the next of kin before they can proceed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Only clinical autopsies require consent. Medico-legal autopsies are ordered by legal authority under CrPC provisions and proceed without consent of relatives.

answers.text: A clinical autopsy is performed to determine the manner of death for court proceedings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Clinical autopsies serve diagnostic and clinical audit purposes in a hospital setting. Determining the manner of death for court proceedings is the domain of the medico-legal autopsy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: the key distinction is authority and purpose. Medico-legal autopsies are ordered under statutory authority (no consent needed) for forensic and legal purposes; clinical autopsies require consent and serve diagnostic goals.
Well done. Understanding the fundamental distinction between clinical and medico-legal autopsies — authority, consent, and purpose — is the foundation for all forensic autopsy practice.

params.question: What is the primary reason that NHRC guidelines mandate enhanced autopsy protocols for deaths in police custody, beyond a routine medico-legal autopsy?

answers.text: Custodial deaths require a faster turnaround for the post-mortem report to satisfy judicial deadlines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Enhanced protocols are not about speed of reporting. They address the structural conflict of interest where the investigating authority may itself be implicated in the death.

answers.text: The state has an inherent conflict of interest — it bears the duty of care towards those in custody yet is simultaneously the primary suspect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The state has both a constitutional and statutory duty of care towards persons in its custody. When an unnatural death occurs, the state is also the primary suspect — this inherent conflict necessitates independent, enhanced protocols to ensure objectivity.

answers.text: Custodial deaths always involve allegations of poisoning, requiring specialised toxicological examination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Custodial deaths can result from trauma, asphyxia, natural disease, or medical neglect — not specifically poisoning. The enhanced protocols address the conflict of interest in investigation, not any specific mechanism of death.

answers.text: NHRC guidelines apply only to deaths in judicial custody under Supreme Court orders, not to police lock-ups

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. NHRC guidelines cover deaths across all forms of state custody — including police lock-ups, jails, remand homes, and government psychiatric institutions — not only judicial custody.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: the 'special' element in custodial deaths is that the state bears the duty of care yet may be responsible for the death. This inherent conflict of interest is why enhanced, independent autopsy protocols under NHRC guidelines are required.
Excellent. Recognising the structural conflict — the state as both protector and suspect — is key to understanding why routine autopsy protocols are insufficient for custodial deaths.

interactions.label: During Phase 1 (Scene) of the INTERPOL Disaster Victim Identification protocol,

params.question: During Phase 1 (Scene) of the INTERPOL Disaster Victim Identification protocol, what must be completed before any human remains are moved from the disaster site?

answers.text: Relatives must be contacted and brought to the scene to attempt visual identification of remains

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Ante-mortem data collection from relatives occurs in a separate phase, not at the scene. Phase 1 focuses on documenting remains in situ before any disturbance.

answers.text: DNA samples must be collected from all remains and dispatched to the forensic laboratory

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. DNA sampling and detailed post-mortem examination occur during Phase 2, not Phase 1. Phase 1 is scene-level documentation — tagging, numbering, mapping, and photographing before movement.

answers.text: Remains must be tagged, numbered, mapped to their location, and photographed along with associated personal effects

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Phase 1 (Scene) requires that all bodies and body fragments are tagged, numbered, and mapped to their location. The position, condition, and associated personal effects (clothing, jewellery, documents) must be photographed and documented before any remains are moved.

answers.text: The district magistrate must issue an individual inquest order for each body under CrPC Section 176

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The INTERPOL DVI protocol is an international operational standard for systematic scene management, not a legal authorisation mechanism. Individual inquest orders are part of the Indian legal framework, not the DVI Phase 1 procedure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: Phase 1 (Scene) of the INTERPOL DVI protocol requires that all remains are tagged, numbered, mapped to their exact location, and photographed along with personal effects — before any remains are moved from the scene.

Well done. The cardinal rule of DVI Phase 1 is 'document before you disturb' — systematic in-situ tagging, numbering, mapping, and photography preserves the evidentiary chain for all subsequent phases.
